what_it_does: Neuromorphic chips — processors that mimic how biological neurons fire — often run circuits asynchronously, meaning components act whenever their inputs are ready rather than waiting for a shared clock signal. This makes them very energy-efficient for edge AI tasks (AI running on small local devices), but also makes performance very hard to predict: simple high-level simulations can be far off from what the actual transistor-level circuit does. ANGraph converts the intermediate outputs of these high-level simulations into graph form, where nodes represent circuit elements and edges represent signal paths, and trains a Graph Neural Network (GNN) — a neural network that operates on graphs — on over a million examples of real gate-level simulation results. The result is a fast predictor for how long a computation will take and how much power it will draw, which can be used during early chip design without running slow full simulations.
